output.impression: Neuropsychological evaluation demonstrates a predominantly amnestic profile consistent with mild dementia severity. Episodic memory is markedly impaired across both verbal and nonverbal modalities: Hopkins Verbal Learning Test delayed recall at the 2nd percentile with a storage-type pattern (recognition no better than free recall); Brief Visuospatial Memory Test delayed recall at the 8th percentile. Semantic fluency (Category Fluency-Animals, 10th percentile) is mildly impaired. Confrontation naming (Boston Naming Test, 22nd percentile), processing speed (TMT-A), and executive function (TMT-B) are within low-normal range for age and education. Mood screening is negative for depression (GDS 4/15). Overall cognitive profile is consistent with amnestic mild dementia, multi-domain, with predominant episodic memory impairment

results.authors: Jack CR, Bennett DA, Blennow K, et al.
results.summary: Proposes the AT(N) framework classifying AD biologically by amyloid (A), tau (T), and neurodegeneration (N) biomarkers independent of clinical syndrome. A+T+ constitutes Alzheimer's disease pathologic change. Combined with clinical syndrome of MCI or mild dementia, defines early-stage AD. CSF Abeta42 reduction, reduced Abeta42/40 ratio, and elevated p-tau181 are primary biomarkers for A and T classification.
results.title: NIA-AA Research Framework: Toward a biological definition of Alzheimer's disease

results.authors: Petersen RC, Lopez O, Armstrong MJ, et al.
results.summary: Recommends cognitive assessment with MoCA or similar instruments, structural MRI, and metabolic screening labs for patients presenting with cognitive complaints. CSF biomarkers and amyloid PET may be considered for prognostic purposes or diagnostic certainty. Cholinesterase inhibitors are not recommended for MCI but remain standard of care for mild AD dementia.
results.title: Practice guideline update summary: Mild cognitive impairment — Report of the Guideline Development, Dissemination, and Implementation Subcommittee of the American Academy of Neurology

results.authors: Johnson KA, Minoshima S, Bohnen NI, et al.
results.summary: Defines appropriate use of amyloid PET in patients with objectively confirmed cognitive impairment and uncertain etiology despite complete evaluation. Amyloid PET is appropriate when knowledge of amyloid status will alter diagnosis or management. A positive scan indicates moderate-to-frequent neuritic plaque density consistent with neurodegenerative pathology; does not independently diagnose AD dementia.
results.title: Appropriate use criteria for amyloid PET: A report of the Amyloid Imaging Task Force

output.summary: The NIA-AA 2018 ATN framework provides a biological definition of Alzheimer's disease using CSF or PET biomarkers. Combined A+T+ biomarker status with an amnestic mild dementia syndrome fulfills criteria for early-stage Alzheimer's disease. Structural MRI demonstrating medial temporal atrophy (Scheltens MTA ≥2) supports the neurodegeneration (N) arm. AAN 2018 practice guidelines endorse comprehensive cognitive assessment and metabolic screening as the initial workup in suspected dementia. Amyloid PET appropriate use criteria support its use when diagnosis remains uncertain after clinical evaluation and structural imaging.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not attribute the full amnestic syndrome to diabetes or diabetic cognitive dysfunction without completing the dementia biomarker workup
Do not attribute mild hippocampal atrophy on MRI to normal aging without considering Scheltens MTA grade, amnestic profile, and biomarker context
Do not prescribe anticholinergic medications (e.g., diphenhydramine, oxybutynin, tricyclics) which worsen cognition in patients with AD
Do not prescribe benzodiazepines as first-line management of anxiety or insomnia given fall and cognitive risk
Do not start antipsychotics without a clear behavioral indication given the FDA boxed warning for increased mortality in dementia
Do not start memantine monotherapy at the mild stage — memantine is approved for moderate-to-severe AD
required_recommendations: Obtain collateral history from an informant who knows the patient well — informant account is essential in mild dementia when patients minimize deficits
Exclude reversible causes of cognitive decline with screening labs (CBC, CMP, TSH, B12, folate; RPR and HIV given demographic risk profile)
Obtain structural brain MRI with dementia/volumetric protocol to assess medial temporal atrophy and exclude structural mimics
Quantify cognitive impairment with a standardized neuropsychological battery; MMSE alone underestimates impairment — MoCA and domain-specific testing required
Consider the single case-designated optional biomarker route if biological confirmation would change management or uncertainty remains to establish biological diagnosis per NIA-AA 2018 framework
Assess functional safety: driving, medication management, cooking, finances, and need for caregiver supervision
Disclose the diagnosis and discuss prognosis, advance directives, and treatment options with the patient and family

differential.key_features: DLB must be actively excluded by absence of visual hallucinations, parkinsonism, cognitive fluctuations, and REM sleep behavior disorder; no such features are present in this case; amyloid-positive biomarkers do not distinguish DLB from AD since both may be amyloid-positive

Minimal small-vessel disease burden (Fazekas grade 1) with no strategic infarcts; the gradual amnestic-predominant decline and positive amyloid biomarkers argue strongly against pure vascular etiology

No early personality change, disinhibition, or compulsive behaviors; memory is the dominant deficit rather than executive function or language; positive amyloid biomarkers argue against FTLD pathology
Insidious 2-year course with progressive storage-type memory deficit and negative mood screening (GDS 4/15) is not consistent with pseudodementia; positive biomarkers confirm organic pathology

differential.diagnosis: Reversible metabolic or endocrine cognitive impairment
differential.key_features: TSH, B12, folate, CMP, CBC, RPR, and HIV are all normal or at most reflect known diabetes; positive amyloid biomarkers cannot be explained by metabolic mimics

key_clinical_evidence: In this 76-year-old man, the progressive amnestic syndrome, temporoparietal volume loss and the case-designated CSF A+T+ profile support early-stage Alzheimer disease; amyloid PET is not duplicated

The hallmark feature of AD memory impairment is a storage-type deficit — severely impaired delayed recall at the 2nd percentile with no benefit from recognition cueing — reflecting hippocampal dysfunction, not an encoding or retrieval-only problem

Mild hippocampal atrophy on MRI (Scheltens MTA grade 2) may initially be dismissed as normal aging in a 76-year-old; correct interpretation requires integrating the quantitative MTA grade with the amnestic cognitive profile and positive biomarkers

Black and African American patients are disproportionately underrepresented in AD clinical trials and may face diagnostic delays; clinicians should not lower the threshold for biomarker workup based on race or assume vascular causes predominate without completing the standard evaluation

Type 2 diabetes and hypertension increase AD risk but cannot explain the degree of storage-type amnestic impairment or the positive amyloid biomarkers; metabolic optimization is important but does not substitute for the dementia workup

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. James Ellington is a 76-year-old right-handed retired U.S. Postal Service mail carrier who presents to the neurology outpatient clinic accompanied by his wife, Dorothy, for evaluation of progressive memory difficulties over the past two years. Dorothy, who serves as the primary informant, reports that the changes began subtly approximately two years ago when James started repeating questions during the same conversation, which he had never done before. She first attributed this to normal aging but became increasingly concerned over the following year as his forgetfulness became more frequent and disruptive. About a year ago he forgot to attend a standing weekly domino game he had participated in for fifteen years, and he later could not recall that he had ever had such an appointment. He has increasingly relied on his wife to remember medication schedules and doctor appointments. He has missed bill payments on three occasions in the past year, despite having managed the family finances independently for decades. He recently left a pot of red beans simmering on the stove and went to sit outside, unaware he had been cooking. Dorothy now monitors the kitchen closely. He still recognizes family members and familiar neighbors, but has begun calling longtime friends by the wrong names and repeatedly asking Dorothy for reminders about who certain people are. He continues to dress and bathe independently, though Dorothy notes he occasionally puts on the same shirt two days in a row. He navigates familiar routes in the neighborhood without getting lost but has expressed reluctance to drive to unfamiliar places alone. He is mildly frustrated and aware that his memory 'isn't right,' but appears to minimize the degree of impairment when describing it himself. There have been no episodes of visual hallucinations, confusion with fever, personality change, or aggressive behavior. He denies falls, tremor, or difficulty walking. His wife denies any witnessed limb jerking during sleep or acting out of dreams. Mood has been somewhat subdued but he denies persistent sadness or loss of interest in activities he still pursues.

neurological_exam.additional: No paratonic rigidity. No myoclonus. No anosmia formally tested. Wife notes he has repeated the same question about his appointment time four times this morning. She states he has been forgetting names of long-time friends and recently left a pot on the stove. He is mildly frustrated and self-aware about these changes.
